items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

The plan starts with the 1850 census to find a household that could be hers, then searches the county's probate and estate files for the surname Voss from 1839 to 1899, with a browse fallback, a search for her parents' marriage, and checks of the marriage witnesses and the wills and deeds. Next, the searches will run in order, beginning with the 1850 census.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: Caroline was born 1839 in Rowan County (a_001, estimated), so she would be about 11 in 1850. The 1850 federal census is name-searchable (United States, Census, 1850). It names only the head of household, so a household showing a girl of about her age with a head who could be her father identifies a candidate whose estate file the later items must find. It gives no relationship to the head and no birthplace-based proof of parentage; it is a lead, not evidence of parentage. Its result sets the surname and household the probate searches key on.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: The United States Census Mortality Schedule, 1850-1880, is name-searchable and lists persons who died in the census year before each census. If a Voss head of household in item 1 is absent from later censuses, this schedule tests whether he died in a given year, which dates his probate window more closely than the full 1839-1899 span. Negative results do not exclude a father who died without a schedule entry.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: Rowan County Probate Records (1753-1970) is the county's primary estate source for a father's death when no death certificate exists, since North Carolina did not require statewide civil death registration until 1913 (loc_001). Its index is only partly name-indexed (about 40 percent), so a keyword search for the surname Voss across the full 1839-1899 window is more reliable than browsing by year (loc_001 quirk). The window runs to 1899 because a father of a child born in 1839 could die up to roughly 60 years later, and the window is not capped at Caroline's 1858 marriage. Any file naming Caroline or a sibling as heir answers the question directly.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: North Carolina Estate Files, 1663-1979, is name-searchable and holds estate papers statewide, so it can carry a Rowan estate that the county index in item 3 does not name. A search on the surname Voss, filtered to Rowan County and 1839-1899, tests whether an estate file names Caroline or a sibling as an heir. Run alongside item 3, not after it, because the county index is incomplete.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: If the keyword search in item 3 finds no Voss estate, browse the Rowan County probate image group year by year for the same window. The probate collection is browse-only (loc_001), so this is an image browse, not a name search. It covers estates that the partial name index in item 3 does not reach. A file found here naming Caroline's father settles the question once read.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: A dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage. North Carolina Civil Marriages, 1763-1868, is name-searchable and North Carolina Marriages, 1759-1979 is also name-searchable. The couple's marriage confirms them as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name if it was her first marriage, which census and probate records often omit. Its date relative to Caroline's 1839 birth corroborates a father named only by a probate or census. The marriage proves the couple married, not that Caroline is their child; a record placing her with them is still needed. Search both surnames once a candidate father is known from items 1 to 4.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: Friends-and-family search (FAN). The bondsman and witnesses on Caroline's circa 1858 Rowan County marriage record are not yet extracted from src_001; they are often the bride's father or brother. Once read, search each named man's own estate file in the North Carolina Estate Files (name-searchable) for Caroline or a Voss heir. This tests whether the marriage bond points to her father, since a surety is frequently a near relative. It is FAN breadth required for a parentage question, not a search for the bondsman's own facts.

items.jurisdiction: Rowan County, North Carolina, United States
items.rationale: North Carolina, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017, is name-searchable. A father's will may be recorded in a deed book even where the probate file is lost or unindexed, and deed recitals of heirs or adjoining landowners can name Caroline and her siblings. The window follows the father's plausible lifespan, not Caroline's own 1858 marriage. A will or deed naming Caroline as a daughter of a Voss would settle the question once read.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

planItems.rationale: Re-read the full 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (record ark:/61903/1:1:MXYZ, src_001) to capture every member by name, age and birthplace. The logged search (log_001) found Patrick in dwelling 84 but the assertions do not name Thomas's wife or the other children, and those names are needed to plan the parents' marriage and sibling searches. The tree gives Patrick's birthplace as Ireland and his age as about 5 in 1850, which conflicts with the objective's 'born in Pennsylvania'; the household read should record birthplace for each member to test that. Name-searchable collection.

Find Thomas Flynn's household in 1860 with Patrick, the wife and siblings, to place the same child with the same parents a second time. Tree source S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census) is attached to the family but no search for it is logged. The 1860 census names every member, so it can confirm the child-parent link directly, not only by household position. Name-searchable national collection.

Find Thomas Flynn's household in 1870 and 1880 to show whether Thomas and his wife are still living with Patrick and the younger children, and whether Thomas's death is recorded in the household. The 1880 census gives relationship to head, which tests whether Patrick is the son of Thomas. Both are name-searchable national collections. Searching on the wife's given name from item pli_004 narrows the household match.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818) to his wife, the candidate parents. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage; it is not yet known whether she married before, so a surname given in one marriage record is not treated as her birth name. It dates the couple's union against Patrick's birth about 1845, which corroborates the parentage but does not by itself prove that Patrick is their child. Name-searchable county marriage collection; search on Thomas Flynn with the wife's name once pli_004 names her.

Search for Patrick's baptism in a Schuylkill County Catholic register, which would name both parents and the mother's maiden name. This applies only if he was born in Pennsylvania, as the objective states; the tree and the 1850 age point to Ireland, so this item may come up empty. The Pennsylvania births and christenings collection is name-searchable, but sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese (Archdiocese of Philadelphia for Schuylkill), not the county. Use item pli_009 if no entry turns up.

Fallback for pli_008: if Patrick was born in Ireland, as the tree and the 1850 census age indicate, his baptism is in an Irish parish register that names his parents. Pennsylvania has no record of it. The county is unknown and must be fixed from the household record (pli_004) or the death certificate (pli_010) before searching. Irish parish registers are not in the place survey for this project, so search them through an external site and do not assume a county.

Patrick's own death entry: his death on 1908-03-12 is in the tree and is attached as source S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates). Pennsylvania's state certificates from 1906 usually name the decedent's father and mother, which would give the parents directly. Read the attached certificate first, then search the death index for the record's image if it is not already in hand. Name-searchable state deaths collection.

Patrick's burial entry, which the death date may not reveal and which may place him in a family plot with Thomas. The subject died in 1908 and the birth register is not available, so his burial entry is one of the records likely to state a birthplace or a parish. Name-searchable cemetery collection.

Search the Schuylkill County Register of Wills for a will or administration of Thomas Flynn. A probate file names heirs, so it can name Patrick as a son. The date range is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818, so he could have died any time after 1850 and before about 1905), not to the 1845 birth. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the index books, not a name search. Records from 1811 onward are held at the Register of Wills.

Fallback for pli_012: if Thomas's estate was not filed with the Register of Wills or the index browse is inconclusive, the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court holds estate dockets and distributions from 1885. Its distributions list heirs by name. Access is unknown, so confirm the holding before relying on it.

Associates item (FAN): search the baptisms and marriages of Thomas Flynn's other children, and the neighbours and sponsors named in the same registers. A sibling's baptism or marriage names the same parents, which can establish Patrick's mother and father. The 1850 census neighbours of dwelling 84 (from pli_004) are the first FAN names to search. Created the first research plan for who Patrick Flynn's parents were: eleven steps, starting by re-reading the 1850 household to learn Thomas Flynn's wife and children, then the 1860 to 1880 censuses, the parents' marriage, Patrick's baptism (in Pennsylvania or Ireland), his death and burial entries, Thomas's estate records, and relatives' records. The searches will run through FamilySearch first, then the Irish and county record sources where a step needs them.

items.rationale: Re-read the full 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (record ark:/61903/1:1:MXYZ, src_001) to capture every member by name, age and birthplace. The logged search (log_001) found Patrick in dwelling 84 but the assertions do not name Thomas's wife or the other children, and those names are needed to plan the parents' marriage and sibling searches. The tree gives Patrick's birthplace as Ireland and his age as about 5 in 1850, which conflicts with the objective's 'born in Pennsylvania'; the household read should record birthplace for each member to test that. Name-searchable collection.

Find Thomas Flynn's household in 1860 with Patrick, the wife and siblings, to place the same child with the same parents a second time. Tree source S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census) is attached to the family but no search for it is logged. The 1860 census names every member, so it can confirm the child-parent link directly, not only by household position. Name-searchable national collection.

Find Thomas Flynn's household in 1870 and 1880 to show whether Thomas and his wife are still living with Patrick and the younger children, and whether Thomas's death is recorded in the household. The 1880 census gives relationship to head, which tests whether Patrick is the son of Thomas. Both are name-searchable national collections. Searching on the wife's given name from item pli_004 narrows the household match.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818) to his wife, the candidate parents. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage; it is not yet known whether she married before, so a surname given in one marriage record is not treated as her birth name. It dates the couple's union against Patrick's birth about 1845, which corroborates the parentage but does not by itself prove that Patrick is their child. Name-searchable county marriage collection; search on Thomas Flynn with the wife's name once pli_004 names her.

Search for Patrick's baptism in a Schuylkill County Catholic register, which would name both parents and the mother's maiden name. This applies only if he was born in Pennsylvania, as the objective states; the tree and the 1850 age point to Ireland, so this item may come up empty. The Pennsylvania births and christenings collection is name-searchable, but sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese (Archdiocese of Philadelphia for Schuylkill), not the county. Use item pli_009 if no entry turns up.

Fallback for pli_008: if Patrick was born in Ireland, as the tree and the 1850 census age indicate, his baptism is in an Irish parish register that names his parents. Pennsylvania has no record of it. The county is unknown and must be fixed from the household record (pli_004) or the death certificate (pli_010) before searching. Irish parish registers are not in the place survey for this project, so search them through an external site and do not assume a county.

Patrick's own death entry: his death on 1908-03-12 is in the tree and is attached as source S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates). Pennsylvania's state certificates from 1906 usually name the decedent's father and mother, which would give the parents directly. Read the attached certificate first, then search the death index for the record's image if it is not already in hand. Name-searchable state deaths collection.

Patrick's burial entry, which the death date may not reveal and which may place him in a family plot with Thomas. The subject died in 1908 and the birth register is not available, so his burial entry is one of the records likely to state a birthplace or a parish. Name-searchable cemetery collection.

Search the Schuylkill County Register of Wills for a will or administration of Thomas Flynn. A probate file names heirs, so it can name Patrick as a son. The date range is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818, so he could have died any time after 1850 and before about 1905), not to the 1845 birth. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the index books, not a name search. Records from 1811 onward are held at the Register of Wills.

Fallback for pli_012: if Thomas's estate was not filed with the Register of Wills or the index browse is inconclusive, the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court holds estate dockets and distributions from 1885. Its distributions list heirs by name. Access is unknown, so confirm the holding before relying on it.

Associates item (FAN): search the baptisms and marriages of Thomas Flynn's other children, and the neighbours and sponsors named in the same registers. A sibling's baptism or marriage names the same parents, which can establish Patrick's mother and father. The 1850 census neighbours of dwelling 84 (from pli_004) are the first FAN names to search. Name-searchable collections of births and christenings and church marriages.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Henry Mayfield's marriage to the woman in the household gives her given name as the clerk recorded it at the time of the marriage. No Virginia marriage collection for Goochland was confirmed by the catalog this session, so the county courthouse or a name-searchable marriage index is the route. The locality entry lists United States census collections only through 1930, so confirm the 1940 census is available for Goochland before searching it. The 1950 census falls inside the window too, but it is a later enumeration and is not in the locality entry; check its availability with collections_search before planning a search of it. response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

planItems.rationale: Marriage of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania) and Sarah, named as a couple in the tree with no marriage fact or source. The date sets the earliest possible birth of any child of this couple, and the record may give Sarah's maiden name and show whether she had an earlier marriage that could have produced other children. Searched as a name search in Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 (name-searchable; Greene County marriage records survive from 1803 per the locality entry). Repository is FamilySearch; a second marriage index (Ohio, Marriages, 1800-1958) is the fallback if the county set returns nothing.

The 1850 federal census is the first to name every member of a household with age and birthplace, so it is the strongest test for the children living at home. The tree places Mary (about 1836) through Joseph (about 1847) in Greene County; any child born before 1836 or after 1847 who survived to 1850 should be in this household. Name-searchable in United States Census, 1850. Search the Hale household of Thomas and Sarah and read every name in the dwelling. Because the schedule also lists neighbors, the adjoining households are the FAN sources for this item.

The 1840 census names only the head of household, Thomas Hale, and tallies everyone else in age brackets. It cannot name a child, but it shows how many children under 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 14 and so on lived with the couple, which counts against the five known children and flags a possible missing child, for example one born about 1830-1835 before Mary. Name-searchable in United States, Census, 1840. Plan to read the tally for the Hale household and confirm the count against the children the 1850 census names.

The 1860 census names each member of the household with age, which tests for children born after 1850 and for any child who left home between 1850 and 1860 but stayed in the county. Joseph (about 1847) and any younger child should appear here. Name-searchable in United States Census, 1860. Search the Hale household and read every name in the dwelling and the neighboring dwellings.

Thomas died in 1868 (tree death fact, Greene County), so the 1870 census should show Sarah as a widow, possibly in a child's household. Each child still living should be named with age and birthplace, and any child born after 1860 would appear here. Name-searchable in United States, Census, 1870. Search for Sarah Hale, born about the expected year, in Greene County and read the household she is in.

If Sarah lived to 1880, this census records each member's relationship to the head of household, so it can show whether a child is a son or daughter of Sarah living with a relative. It is the last federal census that can find children still living at home after 1870. Name-searchable in United States, Census, 1880. Search for Sarah Hale and any Hale children in Greene County and read each household's relationship column.

A child born before Mary (about 1836) or after Joseph (about 1847) would have a birth or christening entry here. Civil birth registration in Ohio was not statewide until 1867, so for the early years the baptism and christening sets are the main source. Name-searchable in Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms, 1765-1947, and Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962; the county birth collection (Ohio, County Births, 1841-2003) covers later births. Search the surname Hale with the father's name Thomas and the mother's name Sarah, and separately with no given name, reading each Hale birth in the county for a child not among the five known.

A child who died young would not appear in any census after death but would have a death or burial entry, and that entry often names the parents. This item covers Sarah's own death and burial and any Hale death in the county, using Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001, Ohio, Church and Civil Deaths, 1833-1991, and Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 (all name-searchable). Search the surname Hale in Greene County with no given name filter, and read each death for a parent named Thomas and Sarah.

Thomas died in 1868 in Greene County (tree death fact), and his own death or burial entry is planned here as the subject's record. It may name Sarah as surviving spouse and give the children's names or a informant, which would test the household against the census results. Search Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 for Thomas Hale in Greene County in 1868 and, if no death is indexed, Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 for the burial.

An estate file for Thomas (died 1868) would name his heirs, which may include children not in the tree; Sarah's later estate, if she died before 1900, could name the children too. The locality entry says probate for Greene County was held by the Court of Common Pleas until 1852 and by the Greene County Probate Court after, so the 1868 file is in the Probate Court. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only (image browse, not a name search), so the Greene County probate docket for 1868 onward is read page by page. The date range is sized to Sarah's possible survival after 1868.

Fallback for the probate browse: if the probate image browse does not turn up an estate file for Thomas or Sarah, the Ohio, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 collection (name-searchable) may hold a will or a deed of the heirs' division of land. It can name children as heirs or as parties to a deed, which is direct evidence of the family's members.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

## Baiersbronn, Württemberg - 1800s

Church books are on Archion (parish page above).

planItems.rationale: Katharina's baptism about 1843 is the first record that can name her father and mother directly. The locality entry (loc_001) says the Protestant Baiersbronn registers are digitised on Archion, not FamilySearch, so this is a paid-site page search of the parish baptism register, Seeger entries only, and the parent names are read from the entry itself. No FamilySearch collection or volume for this place was found.

Familienregister and marriage register of the Baiersbronn parish, to find the marriage of a Seeger man to the woman who bore Katharina. This supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage; the couple's marriage date only corroborates a parent named from another record and does not by itself prove Katharina is their child. Because the mother's earlier marriages are unknown, the search is keyed on the Seeger surname and on each woman who bore a child in 1842-1844, not on one surname alone.

Sibling and household FAN search: other Seeger baptisms and the Familienregister entries for the same household, plus godparents named in them. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents, or a godparent who is a close kinsman, can establish parentage where Katharina's own entry is unclear. Covers the parish register's full span, as children were baptised over many years.

Katharina's own marriage entry in the Baiersbronn register, which usually states her father's name, her mother's name or her home parish and age. This is an independent route to her parents if the baptism is missing, and it can confirm the baptism's identity.

Katharina's death or burial entry in the Baiersbronn burial register, which can state her age, birthplace and sometimes her parents. Her death date is not in the project, so the range runs from her birth to a generous end year. Plan it because burial entries are the usual route to an origin when the birth record is incomplete.

Fallback for item 1 if no Katharina baptism is found in the Baiersbronn register: the Seeger surname in the neighbouring parishes of the same deanery, since the family may have lived in or moved from a nearby village that the project's Baiersbronn birth place does not reflect. Nothing in the project names such a parish, so this is a contingency only.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

planItems.rationale: Marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, head in 1850 and 1860 with Patrick, age 5 and 15) to his wife, before Patrick's birth ~1845. loc_001: Church Marriages is name-searchable, and County Marriages is name-searchable. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so the marriage may sit under Schuylkill or the parent counties; a Catholic marriage would be in a diocese register, not the county. The couple's marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage. No remarriage is recorded in the tree, so this search keys on Thomas Flynn with the wife's name as found on the 1850 census once read. Corroborates parentage by date only; it does not by itself link Patrick to the couple.

Estate of Thomas Flynn, filed with the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, which holds probate from 1811. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (b. ~1818, so death from about 1845 to 1900), not to the subject's. loc_001 lists the Pennsylvania probate collection as browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's will and administration dockets by Thomas's name. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. Probate is the primary remaining route the proof summary identifies, since the 1850-1860 censuses show household position only.

Fallback for the Thomas Flynn estate browse: a name search of Pennsylvania wills and deeds, which is name-searchable, for a will or deed by Thomas Flynn that names his heirs or a son Patrick. Used if the browse of the Register of Wills dockets finds nothing under Thomas's name or the record is filed under a different county.

Baptism of Patrick Flynn, born ~1845. The 1850 and 1860 censuses give Ireland as birthplace, but the 1908 death certificate gives Pennsylvania (loc_001 flags the Pennsylvania birth-and-christening collection as name-searchable). A baptism naming both parents in a Schuylkill parish would settle the birthplace conflict and the parentage together. The Irish parish baptism cannot be planned from this locality entry, and no Ireland locality survey exists yet.

Death or burial of Thomas Flynn, a name-searchable Pennsylvania deaths-and-burials collection. Burial entries often state an age and a parish, and a Catholic burial record names the family's parish, which leads back to the baptism and marriage registers. Confirms Thomas's death date, which bounds the probate search in the item above.

Mortality schedule for Schuylkill County, a name-searchable Pennsylvania collection for 1850-1880. If Thomas died in those years, the schedule records his death during the census year and may give a birthplace and age that test the Ireland-versus-Pennsylvania question. Used as a check on the death or burial item above.

Marriage of Patrick Flynn to his wife. loc_001 lists the Pennsylvania county marriage collection as name-searchable. A marriage record of the subject often names his parents or birthplace, which is a separate source from the 1908 death certificate that names Thomas Flynn.

Burial of Patrick Flynn, who died 12 March 1908. The Pennsylvania cemetery records collection is name-searchable. A parish burial register or cemetery card may state an age and a parish, and it can sit beside the death certificate's account of his father. This item checks the death certificate's informant (James Brown, son-in-law) against an independent entry.

FAN item: the marriage of Patrick's daughter to James Brown, the death certificate's informant. A daughter's marriage record names her father, Patrick, and sometimes his parents or his birthplace, and the informant's own marriage shows the family circle around Patrick. response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

- The tree records a residence for Michael in Pennsylvania in 1870, with no county named.

- The tree records his occupation as miner in 1882.
- The 1870 census search (log_001) found him as a farmer outside Schuylkill County.
- The 1882 directory search (log_002) found him as a miner in Schuylkill County.

1. **pli_001, 1880 census, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch).** Shows whether he was already in the county and working as a miner before the move, and gives his birthplace and household.
2. **pli_002, 1870 census, the county he left (FamilySearch).** Reads the full household to identify the county and any family that moved with him. The 1870 jurisdiction is unnamed in the tree, so the item says so.

8. **pli_008, FAN item: 1880 census neighbors and boarders (FamilySearch images).** Checks whether families from the same origin moved to the same mining town.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

dimensions.rationale: Most items are clearly tied to the parentage question. dimensions.name: Sequencing logic

Free/indexed FamilySearch sources come before the Utah State Archives item. The date_ranges span from 1895 through 2023, covering the full window of the question. The plan correctly places the birth record search before FAN items that depend on knowing the family context. No item depends on evidence only a later item can supply.

response.objective: Identify the parents of Patrick Flynn, born ca. 1845 in Pennsylvania, died 1908 in Schuylkill County, PA
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.
Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

planItems.rationale: Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845 Ireland per the tree, so age ~35) as an adult, and Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, the tree's candidate father, age ~62) in the same household. The 1850 census (dwelling 84) and 1860 census both place Patrick in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill household, so this item tests whether that household persists. 1880 is the strongest of the three: it records each person's relationship to the head and the birthplace of each person's father and mother, so a Patrick shown as son of Thomas, with Irish-born parents, bears directly on parentage. The collection is name-searchable.

Patrick (age ~25, b. 1840-1850, Ireland) and Thomas Flynn (age ~52) after the 1860 census (which names Patrick age 15 in Thomas's household). Patrick may have left the parental home or married by 1870. 1870 gives no relationship to head, so a match to Thomas rests on surname, age, Irish birthplace and neighbouring households: list the Thomas Flynn household and every Flynn near it, and check for a Patrick in the same dwelling or adjoining dwellings. Treat a household match as a lead until item 1 or item 3 confirms it. Collection is name-searchable.

Patrick as an adult near the end of his life (age ~55; died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County per the death certificate, which names Thomas Flynn as father). 1900 gives the birth month and year, years married, number of children, and the household head's relationship to each member. Search Patrick by birth range 1843-1847 with Irish birthplace, and search Thomas Flynn (age ~82, b. ~1818) in case he is still alive and living with Patrick or a child. Collection is name-searchable.

Associates, for the parentage question: the death certificate of Patrick (1908) names his son-in-law James Brown as informant. A household headed by James Brown in the 1880 or 1900 Schuylkill census may contain Patrick Flynn or Thomas Flynn as a father-in-law or boarder, which would place them together after 1870 without relying on surname alone. Search James Brown with Irish-born or Pennsylvania-born wife in Schuylkill and check each household for a Flynn. Collection is name-searchable.

The candidate parents' marriage to each other, distinct from any census search: Thomas Flynn married Patrick's mother before Patrick's birth (~1845). The marriage record can supply the mother's maiden name and corroborates Thomas as father by date, but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child; that needs a record placing Patrick with both parents (items 1 to 3 or a baptism). Thomas may have married in Ireland before emigrating, in which case the Pennsylvania search will be empty and the item should be closed on that basis. Search the county marriage collection, which is name-searchable, for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill and adjoining counties. Note that the locality's Catholic registers are held by the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Correctness
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: The plan is largely correct and well-grounded in the tree's evidence. The skill correctly identifies the 1883 death entry for Harriet Davis Phipps (S20) already in the tree, notes Peyton R. is named in it, and builds a coherent hypothesis. However, the per-test context specifies that items for 'each parent of the head or spouse who is in the project tree, covering that parent's other marriages' should include Clarisa herself (I6, d. 1830). The plan does not include any item for Clarisa Davis's own records or other marriages — it only covers Peyton's potential second marriage. Additionally, pli_005 (Mary Childs's birth record) is framed as potentially identifying Harriet as Mary's mother or aunt, but the indexed record shows Harriet born ~1800 in Connecticut while Mary was born 1828 — making Harriet too old to be Mary's sister (she'd be ~28 years older), yet the plan treats this as a live candidate without flagging the age gap as a near-contradiction. These are concrete factual gaps rather than stylistic issues.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Completeness

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

response.narrationGuidance: Plain language for someone who has never done genealogy. No identifiers, file names, tool names or field names. Never write GPS, proof, proved or exhaustive: say genealogy standards; call an answer a conclusion when it is well established and a finding otherwise; say what we searched and what we could not reach. Never sound surer than the evidence was rated: say the records show it for a well established fact or relationship, probably for a likely one and possibly for a tentative one, and never write that someone is the parent, spouse or child of another without one of these. Say match or search result, never hit; never write ARK: name the record or link to it. Do not describe your own instructions or checks. Do not narrate between actions; report once when the step is done: what was found, in one paragraph, and what happens next in one sentence.

entry.rationale: Tests whether Harriet is the head's step-mother. The tree records Peyton Randolph Phipps (father of the head; died 2 Feb 1843 at Thompson) as married only to Clarisa Davis, who died 20 Aug 1830, which leaves a window for a second marriage. The tree's attached sources include a 1883 Connecticut death entry for Harriet Davis Phipps, which fits a Harriet born near 1800. A marriage of Peyton R. Phipps to a Harriet Davis in 1830-1843 would make her the head's step-mother and tie her to the Thompson household. Name-searchable: Connecticut, Marriages, 1640-1939 and Connecticut, Vital Records, Prior to 1850. Search the surname as Phipps and as Phillips, and the given name as Peyton or Payton.

Read the attached Connecticut death entry for Harriet Davis Phipps (5 Nov 1883), a source already in the tree in which Peyton R. is named. Its stated age, birthplace, parents and spouse can test whether she was born near 1800, was a Davis by birth, and was married to a Phipps. This is a read of an existing record, not a new search. Confirming those details would connect the 1860 Harriet to the Phipps family.

Mary L Childs, the head's wife (born 6 Jan 1828 at Woodstock, Windham County, per the tree), has no parents in the project tree. Her birth or christening entry is the record most likely to name them. Harriet, born about 1800, may be Mary's mother or aunt. Name-searchable: Connecticut, Births and Christenings, 1649-1906. The Woodstock town name has no standard place in the place index, so the search uses the Windham County jurisdiction from the locality entry.

Read the attached 24 March 1849 Webster marriage entry for Benj. F. Phipps and Mary L. Child, already in the tree, for any parent names given for the bride. Mary's parents are not in the tree. The entry may name them, which would settle whether Harriet is her mother or sister. This is a read of an existing record, not a new search. Name-searchable: Massachusetts Marriages, 1695-1910, 1921-1924. The Webster town name has no standard place in the place index, so the search uses the Worcester County jurisdiction from the locality entry.

Finds Harriet, born about 1800 in Connecticut, in any Thompson household in 1850 other than the Phillips dwelling. 1850 names every member but gives no relationship to the head, so a match places her near the family without stating how she is related. First read the attached 1850 household for the head (Benjamin J Phipps), which may already show her. Name-searchable: United States, Census, 1850.

Read the attached 1870 and 1880 household records for the head (sources already in the tree) to see whether Harriet appears in either. The 1880 census is the first to record each member's relationship to the head, so it can settle whether she is a step-mother, sister or boarder. Name-searchable: United States, Census, 1870 and United States, Census, 1880.

Family and neighbours, a test for identity (BCG Standard 14). Browse the neighbouring dwellings on the 1860 Thompson enumeration page of the Phillips household for Davis or Phipps kin, such as a Davis relative living nearby or a household headed by a Peyton or Clarisa relative. The Phillips entry shows Harriet at the same address, so the page may show who her relatives were in the township. Browse-only images for the page itself; the name index covers the household.

Mode: edit. I added seven plan items to the active plan for q_001 (pl_001: pli_003 to pli_009). Nothing was superseded, and the completed census item (pli_001) and the planned vital-records item (pli_002) are unchanged.

Survey of what the tree already holds:
- The head of the 1860 Thompson household is Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps (I1, b. 30 Jan 1816). His wife is Mary L Childs (I4, b. 6 Jan 1828 Woodstock, m. 24 Mar 1849 Webster, Massachusetts). Mary's parents are not in the tree.
- His father, Peyton Randolph Phipps (I2, b. 1789, d. 2 Feb 1843 Thompson), is recorded only as married to Clarisa Davis (I6, b. 1792, d. 20 Aug 1830). Nothing in the tree shows a second marriage.
- A 1883 Connecticut death entry already attached to the tree names Harriet Davis Phipps, with Peyton R. named in the entry. That fits a Harriet born near 1800, so she may be a second wife of Peyton, the head's step-mother. This is a lead, not a finding.
- The log_013 match is an 1860 entry for Benj Phillips with a Harriet Phillips in the same dwelling. It is a needs-review match under a different surname spelling, and the family structure there is inferred, not stated.

Plan items added (all planned):
- pli_003, marriage, Windham CT, 1830-1843: a second marriage of Peyton R. Phipps to a Harriet Davis, which would make her the head's step-mother.
- pli_004, vital record, 1883: read the attached death entry for Harriet Davis Phipps for age, birthplace, parents and spouse.
- pli_005, vital record, 1826-1829: Mary Childs's birth or christening, which may name her parents, and Harriet may be her mother or aunt.
- pli_006, marriage, 1849: read the attached Webster marriage entry for any parent names given for the bride.
- pli_007, census, 1850 Thompson: find Harriet in another household, after reading the attached 1850 household first.
- pli_008, census, 1870 and 1880: read the attached household records; the 1880 census is the first to give relationship to the head.
- pli_009, census, 1860 Thompson (FamilySearch images): browse neighbouring dwellings for Davis or Phipps kin.

The place index has no entry for Woodstock or Webster, so pli_005 and pli_006 use the county jurisdictions from the locality entry.

Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_003 through pli_009).

---

Harriet is most likely a relative of the head rather than a stranger, and the strongest lead is that she may be the head's step-mother, the widow of his father Peyton. The project does not yet show that, so the plan tests it first, by looking for a marriage of Peyton to a Harriet Davis after his first wife died in 1830, and by reading a 1883 death entry already attached to the tree. Next, the plan checks Mary's own birth record and 1849 marriage record for her parents, then the 1850, 1870 and 1880 censuses for how Harriet is listed and related. The next step is to run these searches in order, starting with the marriage search for Peyton.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The plan is largely correct and well-grounded in the tree's evidence. The skill correctly identifies the 1883 death entry for Harriet Davis Phipps (S20) already in the tree, notes Peyton R. is named in it, and builds a coherent hypothesis. However, the per-test context specifies that items for 'each parent of the head or spouse who is in the project tree, covering that parent's other marriages' should include Clarisa herself (I6, d. 1830). The plan does not include any item for Clarisa Davis's own records or other marriages — it only covers Peyton's potential second marriage. Additionally, pli_005 (Mary Childs's birth record) is framed as potentially identifying Harriet as Mary's mother or aunt, but the indexed record shows Harriet born ~1800 in Connecticut while Mary was born 1828 — making Harriet too old to be Mary's sister (she'd be ~28 years older), yet the plan treats this as a live candidate without flagging the age gap as a near-contradiction. These are concrete factual gaps rather than stylistic issues.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The per-test context requires items for each parent of the head or spouse in the project tree covering their other marriages, including Clarisa Davis (I6). The plan covers Peyton's potential second marriage (pli_003) and Mary's birth/marriage records (pli_005, pli_006), but omits any item for Clarisa Davis's own records or other marriages. The context explicitly names Clarisa as a required candidate. This is a concrete omission of a named required item. The plan is otherwise thorough, covering census records, the existing death entry, and neighborhood browsing.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: The tool calls that are visible all used correct arguments. The place_search calls used reasonable place names and context names (Woodstock/Windham Connecticut, Webster/Worcester Massachusetts) matching the expected predicate of placeName containing '~'. The research_append call correctly targeted pl_001 with seven well-formed plan item entries. The research_query call correctly queried q_001. No fixture_not_found errors occurred.

dimensions.name: Record type selection
dimensions.rationale: Each plan item targets an appropriate record type for its purpose: marriage records (pli_003, pli_006) to find spousal relationships; vital records (pli_004, pli_005) to read existing death/birth entries for biographical details; census records (pli_007, pli_008, pli_009) to locate Harriet in other enumerations and check relationship columns. Each rationale explains what specific information the record type provides — e.g., pli_004 explains the death entry can yield age, birthplace, parents and spouse; pli_008 explains the 1880 census is the first to record relationship to head.

dimensions.name: Objective scope containment
dimensions.rationale: Most items are well-tied to identifying Harriet. However, pli_005 (Mary Childs's birth record) and pli_006 (the 1849 marriage entry) are framed primarily as finding Mary's parents, with Harriet's identification as a secondary benefit. The rationale for pli_005 says 'Harriet, born about 1800, may be Mary's mother or aunt' — but the link to identifying Harriet is left somewhat implicit, and the item's deliverable is partly Mary's own missing parentage facts. The per-test context notes that items for the spouse's birth/marriage record that name parents belong among the first items, which is satisfied, but the rationale could more explicitly state what this would reveal about Harriet specifically.

dimensions.name: Sequencing logic
dimensions.rationale: The sequence is defensible: pli_003 (marriage search for Peyton's second wife) and pli_004 (read existing death entry) come first as the strongest leads; pli_005 and pli_006 (Mary's birth/marriage records) follow; then census searches in pli_007 (1850), pli_008 (1870-1880), and pli_009 (1860 image browse). response.objective: Find all children of Benjamin Fairbanks Phipps, whether recorded in Family Tree or not.
response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.
