response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The 1880 United States, Census collection (name-searchable) gives each member's relationship to the head and the birthplace of each person's father and mother. planItems.rationale: Martha is recorded as 'M J Wood' in Smith County in January 1869 and as a Lanham wife there in 1870 if that marriage is hers. Because the 1869 age conflict (item 1 rationale) is unresolved, search for a Georgia-born Wood or Lanham daughter in general, not only the Martha name.

Candidate-parents' marriage: if the 1860 'M M Wood' household (item 1) is her family, its head and spouse married before Martha was born. planItems.rationale: Martha is styled 'Mattie Landham' at her 31 Jul 1879 marriage to James M Neal (log_001), and that styling implies an earlier husband named Landham whose marriage record would name her under her maiden or first married name. Texas County Marriage Records, 1837-1965 (name-searchable) should be searched for a Landham marriage in this window. Any such record that names the bride's father or gives her birth surname would be direct parentage evidence; a record under a different surname that matches her first husband only partly does not establish her birth family.

FAN item: the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County marriage of W F Lanham to 'M J Wood' (a_004) names the bondsman and witnesses. In Smith County marriage bonds the bondsman is frequently the bride's father or brother, so those names can point to her family of origin. It then checks the marriage records for her possible parents, her earlier marriages under other surnames, the probate files that could name her as an heir, and her death record. Records from Georgia, where she was born, are unlikely to exist for that year, so that item is set aside.

The next step is to search these records in order, starting with the 1860 census for the Wood household in Blount County, Alabama.

items.jurisdiction: Blount County, Alabama, United States (lead), then any Georgia county where a Wood household appears
items.rationale: Tree survey: Martha J Neal (I2) has a birth estimate of about 1859 in Georgia and no parents recorded; the only parentage lead is an uncited tree source naming an 'M M Wood' household in the 1860 census of Blount County, Alabama (volume 005154190, the 1860 United States, Census collection, name-searchable). The 1860 census names every household member and gives birth state, so an infant girl born in Georgia inside a Wood household with a head and spouse named would be direct evidence of who her parents were. The lead is not yet confirmed to be her family, so search the 1860 census nationally for a Wood household with a Georgia-born daughter about one year old, not only in Blount County. Note: the 1869 Smith County marriage of 'M J Wood' (a_004) would put a bride at about age 10 if Martha was born about 1859, so that marriage may belong to another woman; this item does not assume it does.

Martha is in the 1880 household of James M Neal in Hill County after her 31 Jul 1879 marriage to him (log_001). The 1880 United States, Census collection (name-searchable) gives each member's relationship to the head and the birthplace of each person's father and mother. If Martha is listed as a Georgia-born wife, her own entry plus the parent-birthplace fields narrow the parental state, and any stepchild or relative in the same household can point to a family. This item tests what the household itself shows, not the 1879 marriage.

items.jurisdiction: Smith County and Hill County, Texas, United States
items.rationale: Martha is recorded as 'M J Wood' in Smith County in January 1869 and as a Lanham wife there in 1870 if that marriage is hers. The 1870 United States, Census collection (name-searchable) shows whether a Wood household in Smith County or elsewhere in Texas holds a Georgia-born daughter of about ten years, which would connect the 1869 bride to a family of origin. Because the 1869 age conflict (item 1 rationale) is unresolved, search for a Georgia-born Wood or Lanham daughter in general, not only the Martha name.

Candidate-parents' marriage: if the 1860 'M M Wood' household (item 1) is her family, its head and spouse married before Martha was born. Alabama County Marriages 1818-1936 (name-searchable) and the Blount County marriage volumes 1820-1888 (80-100% name-indexed, full-text searchable) should be searched for a Wood marriage in this window. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name and corroborates the couple as a unit, but it does not by itself prove Martha is their child; that needs a record placing her in the household (items 1 and 2). Use only the surname from the 1860 household, not a name from memory.

items.jurisdiction: Texas, United States (Hill and Smith counties first)
items.rationale: Martha is styled 'Mattie Landham' at her 31 Jul 1879 marriage to James M Neal (log_001), and that styling implies an earlier husband named Landham whose marriage record would name her under her maiden or first married name. Texas County Marriage Records, 1837-1965 (name-searchable) should be searched for a Landham marriage in this window. Any such record that names the bride's father or gives her birth surname would be direct parentage evidence; a record under a different surname that matches her first husband only partly does not establish her birth family.

FAN item: the 7 Jan 1869 Smith County marriage of W F Lanham to 'M J Wood' (a_004) names the bondsman and witnesses. In Smith County marriage bonds the bondsman is frequently the bride's father or brother, so those names can point to her family of origin. Smith County marriage volumes 1857-1876 (volume 007255720, 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable) should be searched for any earlier marriage of a bride M J or Martha Wood under any surname, and the bondsmen on the 1869 record should be read from the image. Whatever those witnesses turn out to be, they are leads for item 7, not conclusions.

The window is sized to a father's lifespan from Martha's birth (about 1859 plus roughly 60 years), not to her marriages. Alabama Probate Records, 1809-1985 is browse-only as an index, but its image text is full-text searchable (the Blount probate records are not name-indexed, 0-3%), so the item is a keyword search for the Wood surname together with 'Martha', 'Mattie' or 'daughter' in an estate file. An estate file naming a daughter Martha or Mattie Wood, or her married name, would be direct parentage evidence for a father in the 1860 household.

FAN and parentage: Hill County probate case files 1853-1935 (volume 004820309) are full-text searchable but only about 3% name-indexed, so a keyword search is needed. Search for a Landham or Wood estate naming Martha, Mattie or M J as an heir or for a probate of her father. The window runs from the 1879 marriage forward to 1935 because a father who died after she married would still leave a file. This item tests the Landham styling from item 5 against a probate that might name her birth family.

Martha's own death record and burial: her death is not yet dated in the tree. Texas Deaths, 1890-1977 (name-searchable) and Texas Deaths and Burials, 1903-1973 (name-searchable) should be searched across the surnames she used (Neal, Hamby, Landham, Lanham, Wood) with no date filter on the first pass. A Texas death certificate from 1903 on usually names the decedent's parents and birthplace, so it could give the parents' names directly. The 1888 date is the Hamby marriage, the last marriage known, so death after it is the only window that fits the record set.

Martha's own birth record: she was born about 1859 in Georgia, and no statewide civil birth registration for Georgia covers 1859. No Georgia locality entry exists in research.json, so no birth record for her can be searched; her parents must come from the census, marriage, probate and death items above.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

The tree's only residence fact is 1870 in Muhlenberg County, so 1870 is the last known residence. Finding him in the 1880 federal census (age about 66) tests whether he was still alive and where, which narrows the death window. If he is absent, search the household of each name-variant member and the neighbours in the same enumeration district to see whether a widow or son is listed. Census lists no death date, so this item brackets the death, not dates it.

Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 (collection 1875188) is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's probate volumes for 1870-1895, not a name search. items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

planItems.rationale: Mary Dawson's baptism (birth about 1772) is the record most likely to name her father and mother. The tree holds no parents and no source for her birth (only the starting-point fact 'about 1772, Lincolnshire', not yet checked). The England, Births and Christenings collection (1473014) is name-searchable but is a partial Legacy index (loc_001), so a nil there does not prove no baptism exists; if it comes back empty, the parish register itself must be checked (item 2).

Fallback for item 1. loc_001 says the partial index may omit the baptism, so the original parish register must be browsed for the baptism of a Mary Dawson (or a transcribed Dawson entry) in the parishes of the Lincolnshire area where she was born. The register start date for these parishes is not recorded in the project, so the register may not reach back to 1772 at all; that gap is why item 5 (her burial or death) is also planned.

Parents' marriage, planned as a dedicated item and not folded into the baptism search. No candidate couple is yet known, so search surname Dawson as a wildcard across Lincolnshire marriages 1740-1772 and record each Dawson marriage with its bride. If the bride's name gives a maiden surname, it is her first marriage only if no earlier marriage shows up, so every Dawson marriage found must be checked against the others. The marriage would corroborate a father named by a later record, but it cannot alone establish that Mary is their child; a baptism or a probate naming her is needed for that.

Mary Dawson's own marriage. Marriage entries in English parish registers often name the bride's father, or state the bride's parish of residence, which is a route to her origin. Search with no surname restriction on the bride's given name Mary, and treat any Mary whose age matches about 1772 as a candidate until the match is tested against her baptism.

Mary Dawson's burial or death entry, dated to the years after she was last known alive. Burial entries often give an age and a parish, which can give a birth parish where the baptism cannot be found. Searched without surname filter on a given name Mary, matched against her age and any Dawson household.

Fellow-associate (FAN) search: baptisms of siblings of Mary Dawson, which would name the same parents. Search surname Dawson with any given name, 1760-1790, and check each child's parents against the parents' marriage found in item 3. A sibling's baptism naming a Dawson father and mother who match the household is independent evidence for Mary's parentage that does not depend on her own baptism being indexed.

Probate of a Dawson father or mother naming a daughter Mary. The window is sized to the creator, not to Mary: a parent of a child born about 1772 could have died anywhere from about 1772 to about 1830, so the item covers that span. A will naming Mary as a daughter is direct evidence of parentage, and a will naming a Dawson who is not already known could identify a candidate father.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

## Kongsberg Parish, Buskerud, Norway — Locality Guide (1760–1810)

**Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Kongsberg prestegjeld, Kongsberg prosti, Oslo bispedømme (until 1948). Civil jurisdiction in 1780: Buskerud amt (from 1680), Numedal og Sandsvær sorenskriveri, Kongsberg Byfogderi (probate/skifterett).

### Church Records

All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Browse image by image.

**Key FamilySearch volumes for a ~1780 baptism:**
- **008680156_003** (1769–1782, 382 images) — prime target for a ~1780 birth
- **008680157_002** (1783–1797, 249 images) — wider date window fallback
- **008680157_003** (1795–1816, 380 images)
- **009061212** (Kongsberg + Jondalen combined, 1696–1915, 691 images)

**National indexed extracts (searchable):**
- Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014): 28,370 Kongsberg records — search first; coverage of 1780s may be incomplete
- Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080)
- Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081)
- Same extracts also at Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms col 60092) and MyHeritage

**Digitalarkivet:** Complete parish register scans 1696–1969 at media.digitalarkivet.no (Buskerud county, Kongsberg prestegjeld). Both Kongsberg proper and Jondalen sub-parish registers are available. Same material as FS volumes; browse by year range.

### Census Records
- 1801 census (FS col 3733603, indexed + images; also Digitalarkivet, Ancestry, MyHeritage)
- No pre-1801 national census; the mine rolls below partially fill this gap

### Kongsberg Sølvverk (Silver Mine) Records
Special census-type rolls at Digitalarkivet for mine employees:
- Pensjonister (pensioners) 1711; Borgere (citizens/residents) 1723; Funksjonærer (officials) 1765
These predate the ~1780 birth but may document a father employed at the mine.

### Military / Conscription (Lægdsruller)
Norwegian levy rolls began 1789. A male born ~1780 enrolled ~age 7–9, listed directly **under his father's name** — direct parentage evidence. Access: Digitalarkivet (browse and search) and Riksarkivet physical holdings for Numedal og Sandsvær lægd.

### Probate Records
- Kongsberg Byfogderi Skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 (FS Catalog 437559, browse-only; also Digitalarkivet)
- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306, indexed)
- Kongsberg deanery probate 1741–1816 at Digitalarkivet

### Land and Property
- Pantebøker (mortgage books) 1721–1864 at FamilySearch Catalog (no. 485469, Kongsberg Byfogderi)

## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)

The civil birth registration is the record most likely to name both parents with their ages and birthplaces. The locality entry loc_001 lists Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 as name-searchable. Per the locality quirk, search with the paternal surname Hernández alone; if she is not found, search through a parent once one is named.

The baptism entry (Mexico, Jalisco, Catholic Church Records, 1590-2022, and Mexico, Baptisms, 1560-1950 as the national index) would name the parents and godparents. It is the route if no civil birth entry is found, and it corroborates item 1. loc_001 lists both collections as name-searchable. Search with the paternal surname Hernández alone, per the locality quirk, and treat the mother's surname Ramírez as unconfirmed until a record names her.

The parents' marriage (Mexico, Marriages, 1570-1950, and the Jalisco civil and Catholic marriage collections) confirms the couple as a unit and, if it was the mother's first marriage, gives her maiden name. Its date before the subject's birth corroborates the parents. The father's surname should be Hernández, since the subject's first surname is her father's. Because the mother's name is not yet known, search grooms surnamed Hernández with brides in Guadalajara. A surname in one marriage record does not settle a remarriage, so any second marriage found must also be checked. response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

facts.informant: Unknown household member reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The household member who provided the name is unknown. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have read a sign, heard a neighbor, or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn or wife)
facts.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by a household member — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. Proximity is 'household_member' rather than 'unknown' because these facts could only come from someone in the household.

facts.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)
facts.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

facts.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
facts.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
facts.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

planItems.repository: Pennsylvania Department of Health (state death certificate)
planItems.rationale: The tree gives Patrick Flynn's death as 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (F2, source S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates), and that source is attached but no assertion has been extracted from it. A 1908 death falls after statewide registration began in 1906, so the state certificate exists and usually names the decedent's father and mother. This is the most direct record for the parents' names. Access is unknown in the locality entry, so confirm it before searching.

The 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84) lists a Patrick aged 5 (log_001, a_001 to a_004). Thomas is in the project tree as I2, born about 1818 in Ireland, from the starting tree and not yet checked (F3). The 1860 census is name-searchable and should show whether the same Thomas is still the head with Patrick, and name the wife who is the mother. The 1850 census does not state relationships, so the parent-child link (R1, found in a record, not yet checked) is still inferred. This item tests it.

The 1880 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household. If Patrick, about 35, is listed as a son of a head named Thomas Flynn, that is a recorded relationship rather than an inference from household position. It is name-searchable as a national collection. The item is also a check that the Thomas in the household is the Thomas in I2.

A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. It is dated before Patrick's birth of about 1845. Pennsylvania County Marriages and Church Marriages are name-searchable. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland or in another county, so a negative result here does not rule out the couple. The mother's maiden name is supplied only if this was her first marriage. Each marriage record found for Thomas's wife must be searched, not only the first one. The mother's name is not yet known to the project, so the search is keyed on Thomas Flynn and the surname of any woman he married in the period.

The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland (F1, source S1), so no Pennsylvania baptism is assumed. The statewide Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable, and a christening entry that names Thomas and the mother as parents would be direct parentage evidence if the family was already in Pennsylvania. The locality entry gives no register start date for the Schuylkill parishes, so a negative result is not decisive. An Irish baptism is not covered by any locality entry in this project and is a separate search.

A will or administration of Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. Its date range comes from the creator's lifespan, not the subject's. Thomas was born about 1818, so his estate could be filed from after Patrick's birth to about age 82. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only in this project, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill Register of Wills books, not a name search. Probate here is a primary parentage source per the locality entry.

Fallback if the Register of Wills item finds no will or administration. The orphans' court kept estate dockets and distributions from 1885, and they can name the heirs of Thomas Flynn, if he died in that span. The date range is from the creator's lifespan, as in the probate item. Access is unknown in the locality entry, so confirm it before searching.

Friends and neighbours (FAN) item, required on a parentage question. Search the 1850 census for other Flynn and Irish-born households close to dwelling 84, in Schuylkill County. The aim is to find kin, such as a brother of Thomas or the wife's family, whose records could name Thomas and the mother, and possible godparents or witnesses. The 1850 collection is name-searchable and was already searched for Patrick (log_001). This item is about the neighbours, not about Patrick's own entry.

Mode: create. I wrote a new active plan for question q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?" No earlier plan existed for this question.

Survey facts the plan rests on:
- The tree gives Patrick's birth as about 1845 in Ireland (F1, source S1) and his death as 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County (F2, source S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates). The death certificate source is attached but no assertion has been extracted from it.
- Thomas Flynn (I2) is in the tree with a birth of about 1818 in Ireland, from the starting tree and not yet checked (F3). The parent-child link (R1) is found in a record but not yet checked.
- The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick, age 5, in the household of Thomas Flynn at dwelling 84 in Schuylkill County. That log entry was made under the q_002 plan. The parent-child relationship from it is an inference, since the 1850 census does not state relationships.
- No FamilySearch ark appears for Patrick in the tree read, so no pending-hints item was added.

Plan pl_002 items, in execution order:
1. pli_004 (vital record, 1908): Patrick's state death certificate, Pennsylvania Department of Health. Most direct source for the parents' names. Access is unknown in the locality entry.
2. pli_005 (census, 1860): Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Tests whether the Thomas of 1850 is the tree's Thomas and names the mother.
3. pli_006 (census, 1880): Patrick's household, FamilySearch. The first census with relationship to head, so it can show whether Patrick is recorded as Thomas's son.
4. pli_007 (marriage, 1835-1846): Thomas Flynn's marriage to the mother, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. This is the required dedicated parents' marriage item. It covers each marriage of the mother, since her maiden name is only supplied by a first marriage.
5. pli_008 (church, 1840-1850): Pennsylvania christening of Patrick naming his parents, FamilySearch. No Pennsylvania baptism is assumed, since the tree gives an Irish birth.
6. pli_009 (probate, 1840-1900): Thomas Flynn's will or administration at the Schuylkill Register of Wills, FamilySearch images. This is a browse-only image search. The date range runs from the creator's lifespan.
7. pli_010 (court, 1885-1925): Schuylkill Orphans' Court estate dockets. This is the fallback for pli_009.
8. pli_011 (census, 1850): Neighbouring Flynn and Irish-born households near dwelling 84. This is the required friends, neighbours and associates item for a parentage question.

Nothing was superseded, and the plan leaves the question's own status and the older q_002 plan as they are.

Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items, and search-external-sites for any item that is not on FamilySearch.

---

The plan for Patrick Flynn's parents starts with the record most likely to name them directly, his 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate, which the project already cites but has not read. It then checks whether the Thomas Flynn in the 1850 Schuylkill household is the same man in the tree, through the 1860 and 1880 censuses, and looks for the marriage of Thomas and his wife, Patrick's christening, Thomas's will or estate, and the families of Thomas's neighbours. The next step is to search the death certificate and the 1860 census for Thomas Flynn's household.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

planItems.rationale: Supersedes pl_002, whose probate item (pli_006) was dated 1870-1890. A reference now puts Thomas Flynn's death around 1865, and the 1860 census still shows him alive with Patrick, age 15, in Schuylkill County, so the death falls after that census and within 1860-1870. A will or administration of Thomas naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county Register of Wills dockets for 1860-1870, not a name search. Probate is held by the county from 1811, so the jurisdiction is Schuylkill County alone.

Fallback if the probate browse yields no will for Thomas. If he died intestate, the Orphans' Court handled administration and guardianship of minor children, and a petition may name Patrick and his younger siblings James and Mary as heirs. Patrick was about 20 in 1865, so the guardianship papers matter most for James and Mary.

Widow test. Name-searchable United States Census 1870 for Schuylkill County. If Thomas died about 1865, a 1870 household headed by a widow (Mary or another name) with Patrick, James and Mary as members, and no Thomas, would support the 1865 death. The 1870 census does not give relationship to head, so household membership by name and age is the test, not the relationship.

Burial record for Thomas, since Pennsylvania statewide death registration did not begin until 1906 and a death of about 1865 rests on church and cemetery records. Name-searchable Pennsylvania cemetery records and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials collections. A burial entry may give the exact death date and the age, which bears on Thomas's birth around 1818 in Ireland. The tree's St. Mary's Catholic Church (Pottsville) baptismal source is a lead: its burial register would sit with the parish, not the county.

Context for a death in 1865 during the Civil War. Name-searchable Pennsylvania Register of Military Volunteers, 1861-1865. Tests whether Thomas died in service, and whether Patrick, then 16 to 20, enlisted. A volunteer entry gives age and birthplace, which would test identity against the 1850 and 1860 census entries.

Family-and-neighbors item. The Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable. After a death about 1865, the widow or heirs typically conveyed or inherited land, and a deed names them with their relationship to the grantor, and its boundary recital names adjoining owners who may be kin. A deed naming Patrick, James or Mary with Thomas as the decedent would bear on parentage.

Required for parentage: the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. about 1818, Ireland) to the mother of his children. Name-searchable Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991. The date falls before the 1860-1870 window because a marriage before Patrick's birth around 1845 is what the parentage question needs. The record supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so the item tests that too. If the couple married in Ireland before emigrating, this item falls back to Irish parish registers, which are not in the locality survey.

planItems.rationale: The tree has Josiah born about 1828 in Ohio and dies in Vigo County, Indiana in 1879, with no residence recorded before 1862. The 1850 census (United States Census, 1850, name-searchable) is the first place he can be found with a household. Search Vigo County first, then Ohio if he is absent, because his 1850 location is unknown. The 1850 census names every household member but states no relationships, so each co-resident's relationship must be inferred from age and surname, not read from the schedule.

The 1860 census (United States Census, 1860, name-searchable) falls inside the 1850-1865 window and places him with a household. Search by name and by the birth range re-derived from the 1850 age, with Ohio birthplace. Then read every member of his household, since the 1860 schedule also names no relationships. Co-residents are the answer to the with-whom part of the question.

The tree records military service 1862-1865 in Indiana with no source attached. Indiana Military Discharges, ca.1864-ca.1985 (name-searchable) and the US Civil War and Later Pension Files, 1861-1934 (name-searchable) both state residence at enlistment or discharge and, in pension declarations, the household and family members. The pension file's date range runs to 1934 because its later declarations testify to the 1862-1865 period. Use these to fix his county and town during the war years.

Indiana Voter Registers, 1850-1931 (name-searchable) list voters by township or precinct and so give residence in each election year. Search for Josiah Rowe across the window to confirm his place of residence between census years, and to test whether he stayed in one township.

A marriage in this window would name a wife and place the couple in a household, which answers the with-whom part. Indiana Marriages, 1811-2019 (name-searchable) is the first search. The locality entry says the Vigo County marriage register is not indexed in a collection it surfaced, so the county clerk's marriage books are the fallback. Search for the marriage on both routes and note which county and year it was registered in.

Vigo County deed and land records from the county recorder can show where Josiah owned or rented property in the window. Deeds name adjoining landowners, which also supplies FAN names. The locality entry does not list a land collection, so this item is a county recorder search, not a collection id.

planItems.jurisdiction: Terre Haute, Vigo County, Indiana, United States
planItems.rationale: United States City and Business Directories (name-searchable) can place Josiah at a street address or trade in Terre Haute in the window. The directory entries also name other residents who may appear in his household or on his block, which is the FAN test for co-residence.

The tree records his death in Vigo County in 1879. Indiana kept no statewide death registration before 1882, so Indiana Deaths and Burials, 1750-1993 (name-searchable) and county burial records are the field. A death entry names the household or survivors and the last residence, which corroborates the 1850-1865 residence reached by the census items. This item is dated after the window and is included only as the last-known anchor.

response.boundedRequest: For the research router only; an agent it spawned ignores this and does its own task. A researcher message asking for one thing (one record such as a birth, marriage, death or census entry, or when or where one event happened; a person's children or siblings, or whether they are complete; a transcription; a letter; a review of attached sources) is a bounded request. A message that asks to research something else instead of the project's current question is not one: it is a different question (research/SKILL.md, "A genuinely different question"). A bounded request's owning agent runs in this turn, after init-project when there is no project yet, and the turn never runs question-selection. A bounded request that asks for more than one thing runs only the first one's agent this turn and names the rest. For a record, or for a person's children or siblings, that agent is search-records, and its turn ends on search-records' "Continue with …?" offer. For a review of attached sources that agent is source-evaluation, which reads them: the router reads none of them itself, and its turn ends on that review and an offer of the next step. A requested record that attachedSources already lists is not searched for: read it with person_read and name it. A children or siblings ask starts from what is attached: the brief tells search-records to read each census attached to the person with record_read before any search (tree_query gives each source's url, which record_read takes as recordId) and to name the household each shows.
